cards.question: List the steps of a simple web server.
cards.answer: Accept conn → read request → parse → find file → compute header → send header → send file/error.
distractors: Parse → accept conn → send file → read request → compute header.

cards.question: Which web server steps are CPU-bound?
cards.answer: Parsing the request and computing the header.
distractors: Accepting the connection and reading the request.
Finding and reading the file.
Sending the header and the file.

cards.question: Which web server steps may block?
cards.answer: Network steps (accept, read, send) and disk steps (find/read file).
distractors: Only parsing the request.
Only computing the header.
None; web servers never block.

cards.question: When won't a "blocking" web server step actually block?
cards.answer: When the data is already there (connection pending, file cached in memory).
distractors: Never; these steps always block.
Only when the CPU is idle.
When the request is very large.

cards.question: What is the main benefit of a multi-process web server?
cards.answer: Simplicity: write one process correctly, then run many copies.
distractors: Lowest memory use of all designs.
Cheapest context switches.
Easy sharing of state between workers.

cards.question: Name 3 drawbacks of a multi-process web server.
cards.answer: High memory use, costly context switches, and expensive shared state/IPC.

distractors: Hard synchronization, needs kernel thread support, no isolation.
Blocking I/O stalls everything, complex event routing, one CPU only.
Too little memory, no caching, no concurrency.

cards.question: Name 3 benefits of a multi-threaded web server.
cards.answer: Shared address space, cheap context switches, and lower memory use.
distractors: Full isolation, no synchronization, simple code.
No context switches, no locking, one thread.
Separate address spaces, cheap IPC, easy debugging.

cards.question: Name 2 drawbacks of a multi-threaded web server.
cards.answer: Explicit synchronization is harder to program, and it needs OS thread support.
distractors: High memory use and costly process switches.
One blocking call stalls every request.
It can't use more than one CPU.

cards.question: How many processes and threads does an event-driven server use?
cards.answer: One address space (process), one thread of control.
distractors: One process with one thread per request.
Many processes, one thread each.
One process per CPU, many threads each.

cards.question: What is the core loop of an event-driven server?
cards.answer: An event dispatcher that waits for events and calls the matching handler.
distractors: A boss thread handing requests to worker threads.
A pipeline of stages, one thread each.
A pool of processes, one per request.

cards.question: Name 3 kinds of events in an event-driven web server.
cards.answer: Client request arrives, send completes, disk read completes.
distractors: Thread created, thread joined, thread exits.
Mutex locked, mutex unlocked, CV signaled.
Page fault, TLB miss, cache miss.

cards.question: What is "calling a handler" in an event-driven server?
cards.answer: Jumping to the handler's code in the same address space.
distractors: Creating a new thread to run the handler.
Sending an IPC message to another process.
Making a system call to the kernel.

cards.question: In an event-driven server, what must a handler do when it reaches an operation that would block?
cards.answer: Start the operation, then return to the dispatcher right away.
cards.memory: Handlers run to completion. They never sit and wait.
distractors: Block until the operation completes.
Fork a helper and wait for it.
Spin until the data is ready.

cards.question: How does a single-threaded event-driven server achieve concurrency?
cards.answer: It interleaves the steps of many requests in one execution context.
distractors: It creates a thread for each request behind the scenes.
It processes requests strictly one at a time, start to finish.
It relies on the kernel to run handlers in parallel.

cards.question: When does it pay off to context switch to another thread while one thread waits?
cards.answer: When the wait is longer than 2× the context-switch time.
distractors: Always, whenever a thread waits at all.
When the wait is shorter than the context-switch time.
Only on multi-CPU systems.

cards.question: Why is event-driven better than threads when there's no idle waiting?
cards.answer: Context switches would just waste cycles that could process requests.
distractors: Threads can't handle network I/O.
Event-driven servers use more CPUs.
Threads require more disk I/O.

cards.question: How is the event-driven model used on multiple CPUs?
cards.answer: Run one event-driven process per CPU; events must be steered to the right one.
distractors: It can't be; it's limited to one CPU.
Run one thread per event across all CPUs.
Use a single dispatcher that locks every handler.

cards.question: Sockets and files share what OS data structure?
cards.answer: The file descriptor
distractors: The page table entry
The process control block
The inode

cards.question: Which syscalls find a file descriptor that has input?
cards.answer: select() and poll()
distractors: read() and write()
accept() and listen()
wait() and signal()

cards.question: What is the weakness of select/poll?
cards.answer: They scan a long list of FDs, and few of them are ready.
distractors: They block the calling process forever.
They only work for files, not sockets.
They can only watch one FD at a time.

cards.question: What Linux API fixes select/poll's scanning cost?

distractors: kqueue
ioctl
aio_read

cards.question: Name 3 benefits of the event-driven model.
cards.answer: No context switches, smaller memory footprint, no synchronization needed.
distractors: Full isolation, easy debugging, and parallelism.
No I/O blocking, unlimited CPUs, no caching needed.
Cheaper IPC, separate address spaces, and simple locks.

cards.question: What performance cost does an event-driven server still pay?
cards.answer: Some loss of locality/cache pollution from jumping between handlers (much less than a full context switch).
distractors: A full context switch between every event.
Lock contention on every handler.
Copying every request through the kernel.

cards.question: What is the main risk in a pure event-driven server?
cards.answer: One blocking I/O call in a handler blocks the whole process.
distractors: Too many threads compete for the CPU.
Handlers deadlock on shared mutexes.
The process runs out of memory for stacks.

cards.question: What is asynchronous I/O?
cards.answer: The call returns immediately; the kernel/device finishes the I/O and the caller checks back later.
distractors: The caller blocks until the I/O finishes.
The I/O is performed by the CPU instruction by instruction.
The data is read ahead of time on every call.

cards.question: What makes asynchronous I/O possible?
cards.answer: A multithreaded kernel (or a smart device) does the waiting instead of the caller.
distractors: A single-threaded kernel.
Disabling interrupts during I/O.
A larger CPU cache.

cards.question: In the Flash design, what is a helper?
cards.answer: A separate process/thread that performs blocking I/O on behalf of the dispatcher.
distractors: The main event dispatcher loop.
A handler that parses HTTP requests.
A thread that monitors CPU usage.

cards.question: In Flash's design, how do helpers communicate with the event dispatcher?
cards.answer: Sockets or pipes, which are FDs so select/poll can watch them.
distractors: Shared memory with mutexes.
Signals only.
Direct function calls.

cards.question: What does AMPED stand for?
cards.answer: Asymmetric Multi-Process Event-Driven

distractors: Asynchronous Multi-Process Event Dispatcher
Adaptive Multi-Pipeline Event-Driven
Asymmetric Memory-Pooled Event Dispatcher

cards.question: Why did Flash use helper processes instead of threads?
cards.answer: Not all kernels at the time were multithreaded.
distractors: Processes are faster than threads.
Threads can't do disk I/O.
Processes use less memory than threads.

cards.question: What is the thread-based version of AMPED called?
cards.answer: AMTED (Asymmetric Multi-Threaded Event-Driven)
distractors: SPED
AMPTD
MTED

distractors: Helpers don't need stacks.
AMPED uses only one process total.
AMPED stores no file data in memory.

cards.answer: It fits server-type apps only, and routing events on multi-CPU systems is complex.
distractors: High memory use, and costly context switches for every request.
It can't do disk I/O, and it has no caching.
It needs many threads, and heavy locking.

cards.question: Which model likely needs the least memory: boss-worker, pipeline, or event-driven?
cards.answer: Event-driven
distractors: Boss-worker
Pipeline

distractors: Network sends.
CPU-bound HTTP parsing.
Database queries.

select()
stat()

With sendfile() directly to the socket.

distractors: Caching file contents in memory.
Caching CPU instructions in the L1 cache.
Storing TCP connections for reuse.

distractors: Interrupt coalescing and TCP offload.

Polling the NIC and disabling interrupts.

distractors: A single-process event-driven server.
